title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - All Critical Infrastructure
description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_otthreatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to otthreatfeed.com and to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: UK government confirms a cyberattack took a generator offline — and is rewriting the sector’s cyber rules
items.content_text: A small UK generating site was taken offline for four days, in what officials describe as the first successful cyberattack of its kind on British energy infrastructure. The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero confirms a cyberattack impacted a small-scale energy generator, stresses the national grid was never at risk, and — the part defenders should note — says sector cybersecurity regulations are now being updated. Coverage widened on 24 August without adding technical detail: the four-day duration and the Iran attribution remain press-sourced, and the NCSC has not commented. The affected site sat below the threshold at which generators must report cyber incidents. That exposed population is embedded generation, CHP and district energy, standby and peaking plant, battery storage and small renewables — unmanned assets reached through vendor remote access or a cellular router, sitting under the regulatory floor. Regulators are now moving that floor.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: On-record statement from the UK Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, reported via SecurityWeek, CNBC, New Civil Engineer, Irish Times and IBTimes UK; duration and attribution from Sunday Telegraph
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Telegraph report published 22 Aug 2026; DESNZ statement and CEO briefing 23 Aug 2026; trade-press and international pickup 24 Aug 2026; re-verified 25 Aug 2026 18:15 ET with no new detail released; attack reported as occurring in July 2026, exact date not published

items.title: The S7 advisory’s real finding: attackers are running AI-written exploitation scripts dressed up as OT monitoring tools
items.content_text: Joint advisory AA26-231A, published 19 August by NSA, CISA, the FBI, DOE and EPA, says threat actors are running AI-generated Python scripts — packaged to look like ordinary OT monitoring software — to find and reach Siemens S7 controllers across US critical infrastructure. The tooling is built on the snap7.dll and python-snap7 libraries and speaks S7comm, giving read and write access to PLC memory, configuration data and ladder logic. Targets are located through internet-wide scanning services, then reached through exposed interfaces, outdated firmware or weak authentication. S7-200, S7-300, S7-400, S7-1200 and S7-1500 are all named, across critical manufacturing, energy, water and wastewater, chemical, food and agriculture, and commercial facilities. The agencies assess the activity as persistent reconnaissance and capability development positioning actors for later disruption, say the targeting is broader than Siemens, and state plainly that this is not a theoretical risk. The related campaign against water-sector controllers is where the confirmed damage sits: attackers modified or deleted project-file logic, manipulated HMI and SCADA display data, and disabled shutdown and alarm functions, creating unsafe conditions with no operator notification.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: NSA / CISA / FBI / DOE / EPA joint advisory AA26-231A, building on AA26-097A and the FBI water-sector alert — via CISA, BleepingComputer, Help Net Security
_otthreatfeed.date_note: AA26-231A published 19 Aug 2026, re-verified 24 Aug 2026 22:00 ET; AA26-097A published 7 Apr 2026, updated 22 Jul 2026; 12-state total through 14 Aug 2026

items.title: CERT Polska: an attacker crossed a shared private cellular network from a wind farm into a heating plant and stopped its turbine
items.content_text: After an investigation running more than three months, CERT Polska disclosed on 8 August what it assesses to be the first real-world case of an attacker reaching an OT network through a private APN. The intrusion began at a wind farm’s edge, moved onto a cellular router, and crossed a distribution system operator’s private access point name — a dedicated mobile network the DSO had provisioned with a carrier — into a controller at an entirely unrelated combined heat and power plant. The APN was configured to let arbitrary devices on it talk to one another, so what everyone involved treated as a segmentation boundary behaved as a flat shared LAN. At the CHP plant the attacker stopped a steam turbine and the water treatment system that produces process water, interrupting cogeneration at a facility supplying heat to roughly 50,000 residents. The incident itself occurred on 29 December 2025; the disclosure and the technical detail are new this month, and the design pattern it breaks is one agencies have actively recommended.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CERT Polska incident follow-up report — via Help Net Security, BleepingComputer, SecurityWeek, The Hacker News
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Incident 29 Dec 2025; CERT Polska disclosure 8 Aug 2026; press analysis 11 Aug 2026

items.title: Clop’s PLM extortion campaign names Shell, GE and Philips — and the stolen material is plant drawings and blueprints
items.content_text: Clop has listed more than forty organisations tied to its exploitation of internet-exposed PTC Windchill and FlexPLM, the product lifecycle management platforms used across aerospace, defence, automotive, heavy machinery, medtech and process industry. Shell confirmed on 14 August that it is investigating a potential incident after the gang claimed 89 GB; GE said it is assessing a claim of 391 GB; Philips confirmed a contained compromise with no impact on customer environments against a claim of 13.5 GB. The advertised inventory is backups, project plans, facility photographs, drawings, diagrams and blueprints. The entry point is CVE-2026-12569, an unauthenticated remote code execution flaw in Windchill and FlexPLM rated CVSS 9.8 and reached through deserialisation of untrusted data. No OT or control-system impact has been reported at any victim — this is confidentiality loss, not disruption. The OT relevance is what was taken: PLM holds the as-designed record of your plants, machines and safety systems, and in most organisations it is neither inventoried as an OT-adjacent asset nor covered by an OT threat model. An adversary who has your drawings does not need your network to plan against you. Two developments since: Clop began publishing full victim names on 12 August and has now listed more than forty organisations, among them Ingersoll Rand, Zebra Technologies, Mindray and Largan Precision, while GE has quietly disappeared from the leak site. More consequential for defenders, ReliaQuest reported on 19 August that the implant is purpose-built rather than a generic web shell: it maps the application’s vault, decrypts every credential held in the Windchill keystore and carries a custom Java class loader that lets the operator run further code inside the application process. Those keystore credentials are how PLM talks to the systems around it — directories, file shares, ERP, sometimes engineering workstations — so this stops being only a data-theft story and becomes a credential-compromise one.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Company statements from Shell, GE and Philips; PTC advisory — via BleepingComputer, IndustryWeek, Smart Industry, eSecurity Planet
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Shell confirmation 14 Aug 2026; GE and Philips responses 17–18 Aug 2026; full victim names published from 12 Aug 2026; ReliaQuest implant analysis 19 Aug 2026

items.title: Ransomware at Winnipeg’s Health Sciences Centre took down door access, lifts and central HVAC monitoring
items.content_text: Manitoba’s largest hospital discovered a ransomware attack on 10 August that landed on its facility management systems rather than its clinical estate. Central monitoring of heating, ventilation and cooling was lost, door access and ID card operations were disrupted, and lifts were affected, forcing local monitoring and manual workarounds while teams restored services. Shared Health said in a 17 August update that patient care was not affected. The mechanical plant kept running — what failed was the supervisory layer that watches it and the access control that governs who can reach it. For anyone who has argued that building automation sits outside the OT programme, this is the counter-example to hand to a sceptical executive: a compromise that never touched a clinical system still degraded the physical operation of a Level I facility for days, and the recovery ran on people walking round with keys.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Shared Health Manitoba statements and CBC News reporting — via BankInfoSecurity, DataBreaches.net, Packetlabs
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Discovered 10 Aug 2026; health authority update 17 Aug 2026

items.title: A cyberattack stopped goods leaving eight Ceva warehouses — and the outage ran for weeks
items.content_text: Ceva Logistics, the contract-logistics arm of CMA CGM, had its European operations disrupted on 29 July and was still restoring services nearly two weeks later. Eight warehouses were affected; on 1 August the company told customers that goods held at those sites were not shipping. The downstream list is the interesting part — Dutch retailer Bol, department store De Bijenkorf, eyewear firm Ace & Tate, ING, football club Ajax and Valve’s European hardware business all confirmed impact, several of them also reporting that order and delivery data may have been copied. Ceva says its air, ocean, ground and rail transport management ran normally throughout, so this was contained to contract logistics. Nothing points at warehouse control systems: the conveyors and sorters were not the target. Order processing was, and without it a fulfilment centre is a building full of stock nobody can release.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Ceva customer notifications and statements from Bol, De Bijenkorf and Valve — reported by SecurityWeek, The Record, The Register and Security Affairs
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Disruption began 29 Jul 2026; customers notified 1 Aug 2026; still restoring as of reporting 11–12 Aug 2026

items.title: CISA’s red team walked a water utility’s domain undetected — and the tooling was not the problem
items.content_text: CISA published AA26-237A on 25 August, comparing two red-team assessments run with near-identical tradecraft: one against a government services and facilities organisation, one against a water and wastewater systems entity. Both engagements started with phishing, then escalated using Active Directory weaknesses that are ordinary rather than exotic — a default Machine Account Quota left at 10, and misconfigured Active Directory Certificate Services templates. The outcomes diverged sharply. At the organisation CISA labels A, the team took elevated domain privileges and reached sensitive business systems and cloud resources without ever being caught, despite the organisation running multiple security operations centres and multiple EDR products. The reason CISA gives is worth reading twice: the SOCs did not talk to each other, thousands of false positives from routine business activity buried the real indicators, and analysts had neither escalation procedures nor the authority to act on what they saw. A genuine alert on an SCCM server tied to the red team was written off as a false positive because nobody could work out who owned the host. The other organisation caught and expelled the operators. Same tradecraft, same class of tooling, different people and process.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA advisory AA26-237A — joint red-team assessment findings
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Published 25 Aug 2026

items.title: Forescout counted 4,407 internet-facing Rockwell controllers — and found 22 of them in the cities that were attacked
items.content_text: Vedere Labs ran an internet-wide scan on 3 August and published on 5–6 August: 4,407 Rockwell Automation and Allen-Bradley PLCs answering on EtherNet/IP port 44818 worldwide, 2,844 of them in the United States. Twenty-two sat in cities hit by the water-utility attacks. Nineteen of those 22 appear to run firmware susceptible to CVE-2017-16740, a stack-based buffer overflow in MicroLogix 1400 Series B and C on revision 21.002 and earlier, fixed nine years ago in 21.003. The finding that should change how you hunt is the network path: nineteen of the 22 sat on the same mobile carrier network. This exposure is cellular, not corporate. These are field-deployed controllers at pump stations, lift stations and water towers, backhauled to SCADA over cellular modems that hand them public IP addresses — which means they never appear in a corporate firewall rule review, and your network team may have no record they exist. Forescout also found the usual companions around the same utilities: expired TLS certificates, abandoned remote-access hostnames and forgotten servers.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Forescout Vedere Labs research — via The Hacker News, CyberScoop, Cloud Security Alliance research note
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Scan conducted 3 Aug 2026; findings published 5–6 Aug 2026

items.title: Head Mare broke a videoconferencing server and shipped backdoored client installers to industrial firms
items.content_text: Kaspersky detected activity in July 2026 in which the Head Mare group chained vulnerabilities in unpatched TrueConf videoconferencing servers — tracked as KLCERT-26-057 and KLCERT-26-058, both giving arbitrary code execution with elevated privileges — to replace the legitimate client installers the server distributes with trojanised builds. Users installing what their own corporate server offered them received the PhantomCore backdoor, which handles reconnaissance, credential theft and command and control, and in some cases PhantomGraph, which routes its command traffic through Microsoft OneDrive to blend with normal cloud usage. Targeting spanned instrumentation, electronics, transport, energy, IT and software development companies. Affected versions run to 5.3.9, 5.4.9 and 5.5.5, which the vendor patched on 18 June. The lesson generalises well beyond one product: any internally hosted platform that distributes signed client software — conferencing, remote support, engineering toolchains, HMI runtime deployment — is a trusted distribution point, and compromising it converts your own patch process into the delivery mechanism.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Kaspersky Securelist research — via The Hacker News, BleepingComputer, SC Media
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Activity detected July 2026; vendor patches 18 Jun 2026; research published 20 Aug 2026; CISA KEV addition 20 Aug 2026

items.title: Team82 chained 23 flaws in Copeland refrigeration controllers to root, then warmed a fridge while the display kept reading normal
items.content_text: Claroty’s Team82 disclosed 23 vulnerabilities in the Copeland XWEB Pro supervisory controller family — XWEB300D PRO and XWEB500D PRO — 21 of them rated high severity. The chain starts with a logic flaw in the device’s Lua-based authentication middleware: because any Lua table, including an empty one, evaluates as true, supplying an unrecognised auth_mode returns an empty-but-truthy object and the router waves the request through to the administrative API. A separate predictable password-generation routine yields a deterministic daily administrator credential, giving a second way in. From there Team82 found 19 OS command-injection issues across API and CGI endpoints, all running with elevated privileges, for root-level remote code execution. The part that should interest engineers is the physical demonstration: from a compromised XWEB the researchers drove a serially connected XR60CX field controller over Modbus, disabled the compressor and cooling fans, and simultaneously fed the display the probe’s legitimate reading — so the load spoiled while the temperature record, the same record kept for regulatory compliance, looked clean. Copeland worked with the researchers and shipped firmware 1.13.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Industrial Cyber report on Claroty Team82 research (Amir Zaltzman, Team82 Research blog)
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Team82 research published 9 Aug 2026; press coverage 12 Aug 2026; fixed in firmware 1.13

items.title: Siemens ships ten advisories, including a maximum-severity missing-authentication flaw in SIMATIC IoT2050
items.content_text: The August ICS Patch Tuesday round from Siemens, Schneider Electric and Phoenix Contact is led by a maximum-severity missing-authentication vulnerability in Siemens SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced devices, allowing a remote unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code on the underlying server with elevated privileges. A critical code-execution flaw in Siveillance Video Management Servers follows — a physical security platform that in many plants sits on the same network as the process. Siemens published ten advisories in total, with high-severity issues in Solid Edge, Simcenter Nastran, Siemens License Server, Simcenter Femap, Parasolid and LOGO! Soft Comfort permitting application crashes, arbitrary code execution, privilege escalation, arbitrary file reads or information disclosure. Most of that second tier is engineering-tier software rather than controller firmware, which changes the exposure but not the consequence: an engineering workstation is the shortest path to controller logic in any plant, and the S7 advisory published eight days later is a reminder that controller logic is what the current campaign is after.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Siemens ProductCERT, Schneider Electric CPCERT and Phoenix Contact advisories — via SecurityWeek
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Published 11 Aug 2026

items.title: Six agencies put a name to the crew walking in through unpatched Fortinet boxes — and the entry CVEs are two years old
items.content_text: CISA, the FBI, DC3, the NSA, the Secret Service and the Republic of Korea’s National Police Agency published joint advisory AA26-222A on 10 August, revised 11 August, on Gunra — a ransomware-as-a-service operation that surfaced in April 2025 and now runs a formal affiliate programme. The agencies name healthcare and public health, financial services, government services and facilities, and professional and nonprofit services among the sectors hit worldwide; no confirmed control-system manipulation is reported. The reason it belongs on an OT board is the way in. Affiliates gain initial access by exploiting CVE-2024-55591 and CVE-2025-24472 in internet-facing Fortinet devices — authentication-bypass flaws that have sat in CISA’s KEV catalogue since early 2025. Those are the same appliances that terminate vendor VPNs, integrator tunnels and plant-to-corporate links at a large share of industrial sites. Once inside, the crew exfiltrates and encrypts, then negotiates through a Tor portal.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA/FBI/DC3/NSA/USSS/KNPA joint advisory AA26-222A — corroborated by The Record, The Register and Cybernews
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Published 10 Aug 2026, revised 11 Aug 2026; re-verified 25 Aug 2026 — no update issued since

items.title: Citrix patches a CVSS 9.3 authentication bypass in NetScaler Gateway — the box that fronts most third-party OT access
items.content_text: CVE-2026-19490, disclosed on 19 August, lets an unauthenticated remote attacker bypass authentication through an alternate path on NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway appliances, with no user interaction and no privileges required. Exposure depends on configuration: the appliance must be running as a Gateway — covering SSL VPN, ICA Proxy, CVPN or RDP Proxy — or as an AAA virtual server, and on newer firmware a SAML action must also be configured, while on older firmware the Gateway or AAA role alone is sufficient. Fixed builds are 14.1-73.32 and 13.1-63.21. No in-the-wild exploitation had been observed at disclosure, but researchers are explicit that Citrix appliances historically move from advisory to mass exploitation quickly, and the reason this belongs on an OT board rather than an IT one is positional: NetScaler Gateway is very often the front door through which integrators, OEMs and maintenance contractors reach the plant. An authentication bypass there is an authentication bypass into your remote-access path.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Citrix security bulletin and Rapid7 analysis — via Help Net Security, SecurityWeek, The Hacker News
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Advisory published 19 Aug 2026; vendor guidance reiterated 21 Aug 2026

items.title: FUXA, the free web SCADA/HMI that turns up in small plants everywhere, has an unauthenticated RCE chain under active exploitation
items.content_text: Frangoteam’s FUXA is open-source, browser-based SCADA/HMI software, and its low cost has put it into a great many small utilities, pilot plants, OEM skids and integrator demos that never appear on a corporate asset register. A cluster of vulnerabilities gives unauthenticated remote attackers code execution by more than one route: CVE-2026-25938 bypasses authentication so requests reach the underlying Node-RED execution engine when that plugin is active; CVE-2026-25895 combines missing authentication on a critical function with path traversal in the upload API to write arbitrary files and achieve RCE; CVE-2026-25939 allows unauthenticated creation, modification and deletion of scheduler entries, which is control-system manipulation in its own right before it is ever escalated to code execution. Exploitation attempts against FUXA have been observed, and CISA added a related FUXA flaw to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 19 August with a federal remediation deadline of 2 September. Fixes are in version 1.2.11.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-181-02 and KEV catalogue, GitHub Advisory Database, Frangoteam release notes
_otthreatfeed.date_note: KEV addition 19 Aug 2026, federal remediation deadline 2 Sep 2026; fixes in 1.2.11

items.title: CISA gives federal agencies 72 hours — its shortest possible deadline — on a CVSS 10.0 Oracle web-tier flaw now under attack
items.content_text: CISA added CVE-2026-21962 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 24 August and set a remediation date of 27 August, the tightest window Binding Operational Directive 26-04 permits. The flaw is an improper access control issue in Oracle HTTP Server and the Oracle WebLogic Server Proxy Plug-in for Apache HTTP Server and Microsoft IIS, carrying a CVSS score of 10.0. It is reachable over HTTP by an unauthenticated attacker with no user interaction and no existing privileges, and successful exploitation allows access to the instance or modification of data it fronts. A three-day federal deadline on a vulnerability of this age is the signal worth reading: CISA reserves that window for exploitation it considers both live and consequential. This is not an ICS product, and it is not on your plant floor — but Oracle’s web tier is the reverse proxy in front of a large amount of the middleware industrial organisations depend on: MES and manufacturing execution portals, historian and reporting front ends, asset-management and CMMS webtops, and the ERP layer whose loss is what actually stops production in the Q2 ransomware data. The proxy plug-in is also easy to lose track of, because it is frequently installed as part of an application stack rather than owned by anyone as a discrete asset. This lands on top of a run of confirmed exploitation in the same layer: four KEV entries on 18 August including a wormable Microsoft IKE double-free in IPsec VPN termination and a VMware vCenter path traversal, three on 11 August covering Cisco Secure Firewall ASA and FTD, and two TrueConf Server entries on 20 August tied to the trojanised-installer campaign against industrial firms covered above. None of these are control systems. All of them sit directly beneath one. New on 25 August: SecurityWeek reports the flaw has in fact been exploited since 22 January — CloudSEK honeypots logged attempts within hours of a public proof-of-concept, and SOCRadar tied it in July to a China-linked actor hitting government infrastructure. Oracle patched it in the January 2026 critical patch update. That changes the posture: a proxy that has sat unpatched and reachable for seven months should be treated as already reached, and worked as an intrusion hunt rather than only a patch ticket.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue addition, corroborated by SecurityWeek, The Hacker News and NetSPI
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Added to KEV 24 Aug 2026; federal remediation deadline 27 Aug 2026; exploitation history reported 25 Aug 2026; Oracle fix issued Jan 2026; prior KEV batches 11, 18 and 20 Aug 2026

items.title: CISA’s one new ICS advisory this week is a fire-alarm management console that holds credentials in cleartext memory
items.content_text: ICSA-26-232-01, published 20 August, covers Johnson Controls Simplex Incident Manager at version 2.01 and earlier. Tracked as CVE-2026-27875, the flaw is cleartext storage of sensitive information in memory: while the application runs, user passwords and authentication tokens sit unencrypted in process memory, so a local attacker with low privileges who can dump that memory recovers working credentials for the application and for the systems connected to it. Johnson Controls has issued a fixed release — confirm the exact target version against the vendor bulletin before scheduling the change. CISA lists the product as deployed worldwide across critical manufacturing, commercial facilities, government facilities, transportation systems and energy. The reason to care is where this console sits. Incident Manager federates fire panels across a whole estate, so credentials taken from it are credentials to the life-safety network — the OT nobody puts on the OT asset register, usually managed by facilities rather than by the plant, and frequently running on a shared workstation that several people and a remote support contract can reach. That shared workstation is exactly the local access the vulnerability needs.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-232-01 and Johnson Controls product bulletin
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Published 20 Aug 2026

items.title: DESNZ briefs energy chief executives and says sector cyber regulations are being updated
items.content_text: The most consequential part of the UK generator story for anyone who operates energy assets is not the incident, it is the regulatory response. DESNZ has briefed energy-sector chief executives, issued written guidance on strengthening defences, and officials have indicated that cybersecurity regulations for the sector are being updated. The trigger is instructive: the affected site fell well below the legal threshold at which significant generators must report cyber incidents, and the government source’s own framing was that its capacity was a rounding error against the grid. In other words, the asset that produced a national-level policy response was one the regime had deliberately excluded. Any operator running distributed or small-scale generation should read this as advance notice that the reporting threshold, and likely the associated control expectations, are about to move downward. No draft text or timetable has been published.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: UK Department for Energy Security and Net Zero statements — via Irish Times, IBTimes UK
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Reported 23 Aug 2026

items.title: The legal cover for threat-intelligence sharing expires on 30 September, five weeks out
items.content_text: The Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015 provides the statutory framework, liability protections and legal safeguards under which private organisations share cyber threat indicators and defensive measures with federal agencies and one another. Congress extended it through 30 September 2026 in the appropriations act enacted in February, following a lapse and a run of short-term renewals. That date is now five weeks away, and while there is congressional interest in a longer reauthorisation, nothing has passed. For critical-infrastructure operators the practical exposure sits in the ISAC relationship: the E-ISAC, WaterISAC and Food and Ag-ISAC channels that carry sector-specific OT threat information depend on participants being comfortable that sharing carries protection. The uncertainty is itself the operational problem — counsel who cannot rely on the framework tend to advise sharing less, and the effect shows up before the deadline rather than after it.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Congressional Research Service and legal analyses of the February 2026 extension
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Forward-looking — statutory sunset 30 Sep 2026

items.title: Two CRA dates land five weeks apart: standards adoption on 30 August, then 24-hour exploited-vulnerability reporting from 11 September
items.content_text: The standardisation programme underpinning the EU Cyber Resilience Act sets 30 August 2026 as the latest date for adoption of the horizontal Type A standard and the Type B standards covering vulnerability management. The harder date follows on 11 September 2026, when the CRA’s reporting obligations begin: manufacturers placing products with digital elements on the EU market — explicitly including OT and industrial equipment, embedded systems and networking gear — must notify ENISA and the relevant national CSIRT of an actively exploited vulnerability within 24 hours. Most of the wider CRA obligations do not bite until December 2027, which is why the September date is widely missed. For industrial equipment this is the point at which the CRA stops being an abstraction: IEC 62443 is emerging as the key technical reference for CRA compliance in industrial settings, which means the standard many operators have used as a voluntary maturity model becomes the yardstick their suppliers are measured against in a regulated conformity process. Asset owners are not the regulated party here, but they are the beneficiary — and the practical effect from September is that a vendor learning of exploitation in your installed base is on a clock to tell a regulator, which makes it far harder for that news to reach you late.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: EU Cyber Resilience Act standardisation request status reporting and industrial compliance analyses
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Forward-looking — standards adoption deadline 30 Aug 2026; CRA reporting obligations begin 11 Sep 2026

items.title: A Senate bill would give the EPA explicit authority to inspect water-utility cybersecurity and compel fixes
items.content_text: The legislative answer to the water campaign now has text. Senators Adam Schiff and Amy Klobuchar introduced the Water Cyber Shield Act on 10 August, and its contents matter to any US drinking-water or wastewater operator regardless of how the bill fares. It would let the EPA carry out cybersecurity assessments and require corrective action where it finds significant weaknesses; direct the EPA, working with CISA and NIST, to set tiered cybersecurity standards scaled to utility size; fold cyber risk formally into the risk-and-resilience assessments large systems already file; extend federal incident-reporting duties to state and municipally owned systems currently exempt; add $300 million a year to the State Revolving Funds earmarked for cyber work; and shield submitted security detail from public-records disclosure. The gap it targets is a real one: the EPA is the sector risk-management agency for water but has never had clear authority to mandate cyber controls, which is why an earlier attempt at binding guidance was withdrawn after legal challenge. Nothing is in force. A bill at introduction is not a requirement, and no committee action has been scheduled.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Water Cyber Shield Act bill text and summary — US Senate sponsor release
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Introduced 10 Aug 2026
